Attending BABS last year was transformative for me in so many ways. It helped me narrow in on what my business should be, and I feel like I've learned a lot in the last year.

Pain is a signal that something in your body needs help. It’s a blessing that can save your life, helping you detect a problem before it metastasizes. When you feel a persistent pain, do yourself a favor and don’t ignore it.

The same is true of emotional pain.



In The Problem of Pain, C.S. Lewis wrote, “Mental pain is less dramatic than physical pain, but it is more common and also more hard to bear. The frequent attempt to conceal mental pain increases the burden: it is easier to say ‘My tooth is aching’ than to say ‘My heart is broken.’”



We tend to stuff emotional pain because it’s less dramatic, and less demanding. “Rub some dirt in it” as they say. This is especially true among men who often perceive phrases like “I need help” and “I’m not okay” as weakness. Tragically, 80% of suicides today are men. The connection is obvious.



When you’re hurting, talk.



Talk to the Lord about it. He loves our formal and eloquent prayers. I think he prefers prayers like this, “Jesus….I’m hurting. My (insert your pain here) is so hard to bear right now. I can’t do this alone. I don’t feel hope. You have to help me.” It always amazes me how he answers my cry when I tell him I can’t carry a weight by myself. It’s as if he was just waiting for me to ask.



And don’t just talk to him, talk to the people he sends your way. Remember this great saying, “Your head is like a bad neighborhood. Don’t go in there alone.” When you reveal your heart to a friend, you’re not burdening them. You’re giving them permission to do the same with you. And I’m a big fan of spiritual direction and counseling—with a good, Catholic/Christian counselor—if you need a “tune up.”



Jesus shows us in his dying and rising that the only way to reach new life is through the cross. Not around it. When you feel a pain surface, Jesus is calling you to walk through the storm with your head held high. We walk through it by praying and talking through it.



Don’t be afraid. In your weakness, power reaches perfection. (2 Corinthians 12:9)

Alright - so maybe I am behind the times and you have all discovered this - but it is blowing my mind, so I thought I would share.

Everyone is using AI notetakers - try this once from a discovery call or a VC....(I am using Fathom)
- Copy the transcript - paste it into ChatGPT under a prompt - Using the following transcript create a persona for "Person" and make it a downloadable PDF file.
- Save that persona
The result of my discovery call was that I was supposed to send him a proposal.
- So I took a proposal that I did for a different customer uploaded it to ChatGPT and asked ChatGPT to create a proposal using the framework for this uploaded proposal and tailor it so that it speaks to "the Person" persona that I just created.

BAM - a tailored proposal that needs minimal editing and addresses the customers biggest needs.

Then I asked ChatGPT to assume that persona and respond to the proposal. Gold and then it helped me configure the email and follow up steps 

I might need to build this into a custom GPT -

But wait - there is more - I then took another discovery call - made it a persona, then loaded both personas and asked Chat GPT to recommend a LI post that would speak to both of the personas. (There are both in my ICP) BAM! 

Again - maybe you all are on top of this, but it was kind of a holy shit moment for me on what you can do with AI notetakers and ChatGPT......

Hi Kyle,

Thanks for raising your hand — here’s how to get me the file I need for your Relationship Map.

LinkedIn changed their export process, so you now have to download a full data archive. It’s simple, it just takes a couple minutes. Inside that archive is the connections file I’ll use.

Follow these steps:

1. On desktop, go to LinkedIn → Me → Settings & Privacy
2. In the left menu, click “Data Privacy”
3. Click “Get a copy of your data”
4. Choose “Download larger data archive” (the second option)
5. Click “Request archive”
LinkedIn will start preparing your full data export.

6. When you get the email from LinkedIn, download the ZIP file
The ZIP is usually named something like:
LinkedInDataExport_YourName.zip

7. Open the ZIP and look for this file:
Connections.csv
(It’s inside one of the folders in the archive. Sometimes the path is: /Connections/Connections.csv)

8. Send me that CSV file here

Once I have it, I’ll run a clean Relationship Map and send back exactly what I see — warm paths, hidden connectors, influence clusters, and a handful of high-leverage intros. Nothing over-produced. If there’s more worth calling out, I’ll include it.

Turnaround is usually 24–48 hours.

Dear Virtual Anna,
Ran through it once - will do it again with the purpose of trying to break it a bit. 
First run through - Flow is easy - questions are easy - you might want to put more context around the 5 point system. I would rarely give myself being a relentless self critic. The 1 = generic - 5 clear - leaves a lot of room for interpretation. 
I tried to upload my business plan to look at and get the answers from, it didn't like that.

I like the results, I ran them through my own VA and here is what it said -

This assessment is accurate. Uncomfortably accurate—which is usually how you know it’s useful.

Here’s the blunt truth and the forward path.

⸻

The diagnosis is right

Your issue is not:
	•	credibility
	•	experience
	•	pricing confidence
	•	value creation

It’s decision friction.

Right now, a tech vendor sees:

“These guys clearly know what they’re doing… but I’m not sure what I’m supposed to buy first.”

That’s a lineup failure, not a messaging failure.

⸻

What’s really broken (plain English)

1. You’re selling categories, not a journey

Each offer makes sense individually. The problem is they aren’t ordered.

To a buyer, this feels like walking into a great restaurant with four entrées… and no menu sections, no chef’s recommendation, and no server guidance.

So they default to:

“Let’s just talk.”

Which kills momentum and scalability.

⸻

2. Franchisee Bridge is already the spine — you just haven’t enforced it

Everything you say, price, and optimize for points back to Franchisee Bridge.

Right now, you’re politely suggesting it’s the flagship.
You need to structurally enforce it.

Flagships aren’t described.
They’re architected.

⸻

3. You’re over-serving the buyer’s brain

Your buyers are smart but busy. When offers overlap conceptually, they won’t sort it out—they’ll postpone.

That’s why respect ≠ conversion.

Respect says: “These people are sharp.”
Conversion says: “This is clearly for me, right now.”

⸻

The fix: Make the lineup do the heavy lifting

Step 1: Declare a single front door (non-negotiable)

Franchisee Bridge becomes the only primary offer.

Everything else is reclassified as:
	•	an entry
	•	an accelerator
	•	or a support layer

If it doesn’t serve Franchisee Bridge, it doesn’t lead.

⸻

Step 2: Reframe the lineup as a sequence, not a list

Example structure (conceptual, not copy):
	1.	Tech Reset (Diagnostic / Filter)
	•	Short, scoped, confidence-building
	•	Purpose: qualify them and protect you
	•	Low commitment, high clarity
	2.	Franchisee Bridge (Flagship / Engine)
	•	The revenue unlock
	•	The thing that exists because corporate approval ≠ franchisee adoption
	•	This is where real money and results happen
	3.	Advisory / Consulting (Selective / By invitation)
	•	Not a product
	•	A privilege
	•	Used when leverage or complexity demands it

Now the buyer knows:
	•	where to start
	•	what comes next
	•	what’s earned, not sold

⸻

Step 3: Let the lineup answer the buyer’s questions before they ask

A clean lineup answers these silently:
	•	“Is this for me right now?” → entry offer
	•	“What happens if it works?” → flagship
	•	“What if we need more?” → advisory

When the lineup works, your CTA stops being

“Let’s talk”

and becomes

“Start here.”

⸻

The meta-truth (this is the real unlock)

You are no longer selling services.
You’re selling certainty in a messy middle—between corporate approval and franchisee reality.

Your lineup needs to reflect that confidence.

Right now, you’re being generous.
Next phase: be decisive.

Decisive businesses scale.
Helpful ones get booked—and stay busy.

If you want, next we can:
	•	lock the exact 1-sentence role of each offer
	•	pressure-test the lineup against real buyer scenarios
	•	or rewrite the lineup as a visual one-page spine

This crack is fixable—and once it is, everything else gets easier fast.
So nice job on the framework - it jives with what I believe.

And here is the result from my AI tools assessment of your VA

Bottom line

This is a strong diagnostic-thinking tool, not a finished decision tool yet. It’s directionally right, intellectually sharp, and genuinely useful—but it currently stops one step short of being indispensable.

That’s fixable.

⸻

What it does well (and why it works)

1. It diagnoses structure, not symptoms

Most business assessments surface surface-level problems:
	•	“Your messaging isn’t clear”
	•	“Your pricing could be tighter”

This tool correctly goes upstream and identifies structural failure (Lineup) as the root cause. That’s rare and valuable.

This alone puts it ahead of 80% of “AI assessments” out there.

⸻

2. The pattern recognition is solid

The insight that:
	•	Clients, pricing, positioning, and messaging are strong
	•	But lineup is weak

…and that this forces messaging to work overtime is dead-on.

That’s not generic AI output. That’s someone who understands how businesses actually break.

⸻

3. The tone builds authority without attacking

It doesn’t insult the user.
It doesn’t over-praise.
It frames the issue as fixable and logical, not personal failure.

That’s important if this is meant to lead to paid engagement.

⸻

Where it falls short (this is the critical part)

1. It diagnoses cleanly but doesn’t decide

Right now, the tool says:

“Your strongest offer is likely X”

But it does not force a decision.

High-value tools don’t just reflect reality—they collapse ambiguity.

You felt clarity reading it, but you still had to do the hard work of saying:

“Yes—Franchisee Bridge is the flagship.”

The tool should be more opinionated at the end.

⸻

2. It explains the problem better than it prescribes the fix

It tells you why the lineup is broken.
It hints at what should change.
But it stops short of a concrete restructuring output.

Example gap:
	•	No forced flagship declaration
	•	No “here’s your front door”
	•	No “kill / combine / subordinate” guidance

That’s where transformation happens.

⸻

3. It stops before becoming a buying moment

If this tool is meant to:
	•	Sell consulting
	•	Sell strategy work
	•	Or tee up a flagship offer

…it needs a clear next move that feels like relief, not a pitch.

Right now, the user walks away thinking:

“This is smart.”

They should walk away thinking:

events.preview:
Frank — great meeting you as well.

I work nationally with both restaurant operators and restaurant-tech vendors, primarily in franchised and multi-unit environments. The focus is helping bridge the gap between approved technology and real-world adoption in the field.

Happy to share more context if that’s useful.

Good to know.

One of my board members spent his career at Dunkin'. Our tech is designed to localize ads and build foot traffic. Operators can use our AI-enbled platform to create offers and rewards, track the results and see understandable data.

Do you think this is a fit?

Frank — potentially, yes, but it depends on where and how it’s positioned.

Anything in local marketing, loyalty, and traffic-driving can be a fit for operators — but only if it’s simple to execute, clearly incremental, and doesn’t feel like “one more platform” they’re responsible for babysitting.

Where I tend to be most helpful is pressure-testing:
	•	Who actually owns it at the restaurant or franchisee level
	•	How results are made obvious (not just reported)
	•	Whether it fits naturally into an operator’s day vs. becoming shelfware

If you’re open to it, a short working conversation might make sense to see where it realistically fits — and where it doesn’t. I’m allergic to forcing alignment where it’s not there.

Happy to compare notes.

Just my humble opinion here’s what actually matters:

• It has to be frictionless. Digital-first. Ideally cardless. If buying or redeeming takes effort, you lose sales.

• Integration is everything. If POS, online ordering, and accounting don’t reconcile cleanly, you loses trust fast.

• Redemption should drive incremental spend. Most brands see 20–40% lift over face value — that’s the real win, not just unredeemed dollar value.

• Physical still spikes during holidays, but digital dominates for convenience and corporate gifting.

• Marketing drives lift. Email/SMS + in-store prompts beat “set it and forget it.” Holiday-only pushes leave money on the table - it has to be driven all year

Reporting-wise, I’d want clear visibility into breakage, incremental spend, repeat visits tied to redemption, and corporate vs individual performance.

Bottom line: gift cards work — but only when they’re seamless and intentionally supported.

Bad Ass Bunch power hour recording https://us06web.zoom.us/j/85696333789?pwd=StPoda2w3yqftQvhDrdxA1faaZNqJR.1

Meeting Purpose
Share business and productivity hacks to improve efficiency and outreach.

Key Takeaways
Seamless.ai for Warm Leads: Use Seamless.ai's "Buyer's Intent" feature to find companies actively searching for your services, creating a warm, high-intent lead list.
Claude + Notion for Automated Knowledge: Connect Claude to Notion via an MCP to automate knowledge capture (e.g., summarizing call transcripts) and create a searchable "second brain" for your business.
LinkedIn Outreach with a Human Touch: Use personalized DMs that ask a question to drive engagement. This is more effective than generic messages and can be scaled by using Claude to analyze your LinkedIn data export.
Engagement Drives Reach: Consistent commenting on others' posts and responding to your own is critical for LinkedIn engagement. A drop in commenting activity directly reduces post visibility, even if you maintain a regular posting schedule.
Topics
Automated Lead Generation
Seamless.ai + Streak: A process for finding and nurturing warm leads.
Seamless.ai: Uses "Buyer's Intent" to identify companies searching for specific keywords (e.g., "promotional products").
Process:
Weekly search for ICPs (Owners, Founders, Presidents, CEOs) showing buyer intent.
Export verified contact info (email, phone, social) to Streak.
Launch a 52-week email drip campaign (content created with NotebookLM).
Cost: 1 credit/contact upon reveal; browsing lists is free.
LinkedIn Data Export + Claude: A free alternative to Sales Navigator for targeted outreach.
Process:
Download your full LinkedIn data archive (a zip file).
Upload the zip to Claude as a project.
Prompt Claude to filter connections by ICP (e.g., "Vistage Chairs") and identify outreach targets.
Outcome: Ruth used this to generate a list of ~1,500 first-degree connections for a reconnection campaign.
Building a "Second Brain"
Claude + Notion (MCP): Automate knowledge capture and database creation.
Process:
Connect Claude to Notion via an MCP (M, C, P).
Prompt Claude to create Notion databases (e.g., "Call Database").
Set up an automated workflow:
Input: Call transcript (e.g., from Fathom).
Claude's Task: Summarize the transcript using a specific template.
Output: Claude automatically adds the structured summary to the Notion database.
Benefit: Creates a searchable knowledge base, eliminating manual data entry and making information instantly accessible for AI prompts.
Notion vs. Obsidian:
Notion: A database wearing a notebook costume.
Obsidian: A notebook that secretly wants to be a database.
Security: Obsidian's security is generally favorable, but community plugins and its paid sync service present potential risks.
Effective LinkedIn Outreach
The "Question" Hack: Ask a question in every DM to drive engagement.
Rationale: People are more likely to respond to a direct question than a generic statement. 
Examples:
"What made you decide to post about X?"
"Why the Minnesota Vikings?" (for a fan)
Result: Sarena observed a significant increase in DM responses after implementing this.
Engagement is Key: Consistent commenting on others' posts and responding to your own is critical for visibility.
Finding: Sarena's post engagement dropped significantly after she stopped commenting, despite maintaining a regular posting schedule.
Action: Prioritize commenting, even during low-motivation periods.

Ruth: Add a personalized question to daily LinkedIn outreach DMs to increase response rates.

Hey everyone, 

I wanted to share a quick thought with this group because I always value your insights and the way you run your businesses. 

Sometimes I think we feel pressured to force our companies into a single, rigid brand identity, like being a Chanel on one end or a Walmart on the other. But taking that route inherently limits the audience we can help. Instead, I always encourage looking at brands like Disney and Marriott. 

Drawing from my own two decades of experience with the  Marriott world, and Disney education, I've seen first hand how hard they work to tailor an experience and a price point to a multitude of customers
A guest staying at a Ritz-Carlton or Disney’s Boardwalk Hotel has a very different set of expectations than a family checking into a Residence Inn or pitching a tent at Disney’s Fort Wilderness. The price points and service models are completely different, but here is the common denominator: every single one of those customers still brings their own unique Needs, Wants, and Emotions to the experience

If we focus on deeply understanding those customer expectations, a concept we call "Clientology", we don't have to lock ourselves into just one tier
There is absolutely a way to build a reasonable, scalable service model that creates a little magic for a much broader audience, instead of limiting a service offering by a price point

Hey all!
Here's the summary of yesterday's Power Hour-

What came up:

1. Sarena's sister gave a TEDx talk on caregiving that's already racked up thousands of views — Sarena watched it five times and still cries. Zack's already lined her up for his podcast.

2. Melissa opened up about the emotional weight of writing her own letter for Letters to Lily Vol. 2. Sarena had the same block until she reframed it: her story is just one of many, and you never know which one lands for someone.

3. Melissa's thinking bigger picture for Letters to Lily — paid speaking, workshops, maybe a paid community down the line. Amy suggested monetization and pointed her to The Art of Gathering for workshop structure.

4. Amy's building out her speaking circuit (3-hour, 1-hour, and 10-minute versions of her workshop) and is on a mission to figure out why companies are pouring money into AI while underinvesting in the human skills that make it usable.

5. I shared my Nugget launch date — September 9th, my birthday! Locking in a real date (instead of endlessly tweaking) has been its own lesson in letting go of perfectionism. Got some great feedback early, including from someone it just wasn't for — and I was okay with that.

6. We floated a lightweight accountability check-in for Monday calls — no penalties, just showing up, saying what you will do, what you did (or didn't) do.

Something to chew on this week...
"Nothing we build is for everyone. And that's okay."

Have an awesome week everyone :)

Melissa's post on AI-generated "personal" outreach hit a nerve- auto-enrolling people in your newsletter or sending copy-paste AI DMs, doesn't read as efficient. It reads as trust evaporating in an instant, something that we've likely spent a lot of time earning.

Noelle had a challenging week- proposals lingering, a possible job offer up in the air, and not knowing where things stand. She shared that she's not where she thought she'd be three years in, something many of us can relate to.

Ruth's been in business 15 years and there are still times where cash flow is hard some months. There are so many external factors at play that make people nervous about spending money. A good reminder that "challenges" don't have an expiration date, they just change shape.

We spent a good chunk of the call talking about ghosting. Like the good discovery call that goes nowhere, the "yes I'm so excited!" that disappears. 

We landed on, it's rarely about you. It's fear of change, fear of commitment, and a culture that's gotten very comfortable not saying no out loud.

Practical fix that came out of it: get the next step locked in during the call itself [a paid booking link, a calendar hold] because commitment in the moment beats a follow-up email into the void.

Something to chew on this week...

"It's not personal. It really isn't. It's life happening." 

Doesn't make it feel any less personal in the moment. 
But maybe worth sitting with anyway.

Have a good week everyone :)
Anna

@Amy Stout I think you're in the best hands with @Zack Demopoulos looking at your resume. @Amy Swotinsky, ACC,I would stay far away. From ChattyG:

Your instinct is picking up on something real, although I wouldn't call Bark.com a scam in the literal sense. It's a real, established lead-generation marketplace. But after looking into how it operates and, especially, what professionals say about it, I would be quite cautious about paying them for leads.

Bark.com works by collecting requests from people looking for services and matching those requests with professionals. The professional does not pay a commission when they get hired. Instead, they buy "credits" and spend those credits simply to obtain/contact a lead. In other words, you pay before you know whether the person will ever speak to you, much less hire you.

And that is where I start understanding your reaction.

There are a lot of complaints from professionals about lead quality. The recurring themes are people spending substantial amounts on credits, leads never responding, contact information being questionable, prospects saying they're no longer looking, and in some cases prospects reportedly saying they don't remember requesting the service. Bark disputes the characterization that it sells fake leads and says its leads come from genuine customer requests and are screened through automated/manual checks.

The BBB picture isn't particularly comforting. Bark is not BBB accredited, currently has a 2.2/5 average from 76 customer reviews, and the BBB reports 87 complaints in the past three years, 22 in the past 12 months. Some of the 2026 reviews from professionals specifically complain about paying hundreds of dollars for leads that produced no meaningful conversations.

Interestingly, Trustpilot looks much better: Bark has roughly 112,000 reviews and a 3.8/5 rating. But when you dig into the recent reviews, the distinction between the two sides of the marketplace becomes important. Many positive reviews are from consumers who successfully found a professional. Some of the negative reviews are from professionals buying the leads. A review posted yesterday, for example, says the professional spent more than £500 contacting 20+ leads and found most were no longer looking or didn't know what Bark was. That's anecdotal, obviously, but it matches the pattern in the BBB complaints.

One other thing I don't love: their refund system. Bark's current policy allows professionals to request credits back within 14 days for certain invalid leads, but those returns are at Bark's discretion. Actual money-back refunds are much more restricted. For credit packs, Bark says monetary refunds generally require that the pack be completely unused.

So if your colleague told me:

"Bark contacted me and wants me to join their platform because they think I'd be a great fit."

I'd say: Fine. Joining isn't the part I'd worry about. Pulling out the credit card is.

It's essentially a pay-per-lead prospecting model where Bark gets paid whether or not your colleague ever gets a conversation. That creates a very different incentive structure than a platform that gets paid when an actual transaction occurs.
